steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a computer vision paper about using synthetic multimodal data to detect egocentric human-object interactions in an industrial setting. It should motivate the problem, explain what is missing in prior work, present our data generation pipeline, dataset and detection method, and end with the contributions and an outline of the paper.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Wearable devices and egocentric vision in industrial settings
- HOI detection in prior work; lack of industrial data
- Our idea: synthetic data generation pipeline and tool
- EgoISM-HOI dataset + real test data
- Multimodal EHOI detection method and results
- Contributions; paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Wearable devices and egocentric vision
  - increasingly popular; first-person view of how users interact with the world
  - collect/process visual info hands-free -> natural activities
  - intelligent systems support humans: daily living (cite), cultural sites (cite), industrial scenarios (cite)
  - industry: understand workers' behavior, workplace safety, productivity
  - e.g. detect hands + interacted objects -> monitor object usage, info on procedures, reminders when dangerous objects manipulated
- Prior work on HOI
  - Human-Object Interaction detection (HOI): third-person (cite), first-person (cite)
  - generic scenarios (COCO objects) or class-agnostic settings (cite)
  - industrial contexts understudied: few public datasets (cite)
  - Egocentric Human-Object Interactions (EHOI): need lots of labeled domain-specific data; costly in money/time; privacy constraints, industrial secrets (cite)
- Our idea
  - can synthetic first-person data mitigate need for labeled real data? -> cheaper dataset collection
  - pipeline (Fig. 1) + tool; uses 3D models of target environment and objects
  - many synthetic EHOI images, auto-labeled: hand-object 2D-3D boxes, object categories, hand info (side, contact state, active objects), depth maps, instance segmentation masks
- EgoISM-HOI
  - Egocentric Industrial Synthetic Multimodal dataset for Human-Object Interaction detection
  - photo-realistic, industrial; hands, objects, active objects (= objects user interacts with); class labels, depth maps, instance masks (Fig. 1 (b))
  - real test data: 42 real egocentric videos, industrial laboratory, subjects test/repair electrical boards
  - labels: frames with interactions, active objects with box + class; also hands and all objects
- Method and results
  - does synthetic multimodal data (depth, instance masks) help EHOI detection?
  - approach based on an existing method (cite), uses the multimodal signals
  - beats baselines using class-agnostic models trained on out-of-domain real data
  - good performance with synthetic data + very small amount of real data
  - multimodal signals -> better accuracy and robustness
- Contributions
  - 1) pipeline: 3D models -> thousands of synthetic EHOI images with labels and modalities
  - 2) EgoISM-HOI + manually labeled real images to test generalization
  - 3) EHOI method using depth maps and instance segmentation maps
  - 4) evaluations: synthetic pre-training helps, mainly with limited real data; improvements over class-agnostic SOTA
  - 5) release dataset and code: https://iplab.dmi.unict.it/egoism-hoi
- Organization: Sec 2 related work, 3 pipeline, 4 dataset, 5 method, 6 experiments and ablations, 7 conclusion

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Wearable devices have become more and more popular in recent years, because they give a first-person view of how users interact with the world around them. An advantage of wearable devices is that visual information can be collected and processed without users having to hold any device in their hands, so they can do their activities in a natural way. Intelligent systems can analyze this visual information and provide services that support humans in different domains, for example activities of daily living, cultural sites and industrial scenarios. In the industrial context in particular, egocentric vision can be used to understand how workers behave, to improve safety in the workplace and to increase the overall productivity. For example, if we detect the hands of the workers and find which objects they are interacting with, we can monitor how the objects are used, give information on the procedures that have to be carried out, and improve the safety of the workers by giving reminders when dangerous objects are manipulated.

The problem of Human-Object Interaction detection (HOI) has been studied in previous works, either from the third-person or from the first-person point of view. These works considered generic scenarios (e.g., COCO objects) or class-agnostic settings, but their use in industrial contexts is still understudied, because there are not many public datasets. To develop a system that can detect Egocentric Human-Object Interactions (EHOI) in this context, it is generally necessary to collect and label large amounts of domain-specific data. This can be expensive in terms of costs and time, and it is not always possible because of privacy constraints and industrial secrets.

In this paper we investigate if using synthetic data in first-person vision can reduce the need for labeled real domain-specific data to train models. This would greatly reduce the cost of collecting a suitable dataset for developing models. We propose a pipeline (see Fig. 1) and a tool that use 3D models of the target environment and objects to produce a large number of synthetic EHOI image examples. The images are labeled automatically with several annotations, such as hand-object 2D-3D bounding boxes, object categories, hand information (i.e., hand side, contact state, and associated active objects) and also multimodal signals such as depth maps and instance segmentation masks.

Using the proposed pipeline, we present EgoISM-HOI (Egocentric Industrial Synthetic Multimodal dataset for Human-Object Interaction detection). This is a new photo-realistic dataset of EHOIs in an industrial scenario, and it has rich annotations of hands, objects, and active objects (i.e., the objects the user is interacting with), including class labels, depth maps, and instance segmentation masks (see Fig. 1 (b)). We also want to check if the synthetic data generated with the proposed protocol is suitable for the EHOI detection task on target real data. For this we acquired and labeled 42 real egocentric videos in an industrial laboratory, where different subjects perform test and repair operations on electrical boards. We annotated all the EHOI instances of the images, identifying the frames where interactions happen and all the active objects with a bounding box with the related object class. We also labeled the hands and all the objects in the images.

- Method and results
  - does the synthetic multimodal data (depth maps, instance masks) improve EHOI detection?
  - approach based on an existing method, uses the multimodal signals in our dataset
  - outperforms baselines using class-agnostic models trained on out-of-domain real data
  - good performance with our synthetic data + very small amount of real data
  - multimodal signals -> higher accuracy and robustness
- Contributions
  - 1) pipeline using 3D models -> thousands of synthetic EHOI images with labels and modalities
  - 2) EgoISM-HOI; real-world images manually labeled to test generalization
  - 3) EHOI method exploiting depth maps and instance segmentation maps
  - 4) evaluations: synthetic pre-training helps, mainly with limited real data; improvements over class-agnostic SOTA
  - 5) dataset and code released: https://iplab.dmi.unict.it/egoism-hoi
- Organization: Sec 2 related work, 3 pipeline, 4 dataset, 5 method, 6 experiments/ablations, 7 conclusion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Wearable devices have become more and more popular in recent years, because they give a first-person view of how users interact with the world around them. An advantage of wearable devices is that visual information can be collected and processed without users having to hold any device in their hands, so they can do their activities in a natural way. Intelligent systems can analyze this visual information and provide services that support humans in different domains, for example activities of daily living, cultural sites and industrial scenarios. In the industrial context in particular, egocentric vision can be used to understand how workers behave, to improve safety in the workplace and to increase the overall productivity. For example, if we detect the hands of the workers and find which objects they are interacting with, we can monitor how the objects are used, give information on the procedures that have to be carried out, and improve the safety of the workers by giving reminders when dangerous objects are manipulated.

The problem of Human-Object Interaction detection (HOI) has been studied in previous works, either from the third-person or from the first-person point of view. These works considered generic scenarios (e.g., COCO objects) or class-agnostic settings, but their use in industrial contexts is still understudied, because there are not many public datasets. To develop a system that can detect Egocentric Human-Object Interactions (EHOI) in this context, it is generally necessary to collect and label large amounts of domain-specific data. This can be expensive in terms of costs and time, and it is not always possible because of privacy constraints and industrial secrets.

In this paper we investigate if using synthetic data in first-person vision can reduce the need for labeled real domain-specific data to train models. This would greatly reduce the cost of collecting a suitable dataset for developing models. We propose a pipeline (see Fig. 1) and a tool that use 3D models of the target environment and objects to produce a large number of synthetic EHOI image examples. The images are labeled automatically with several annotations, such as hand-object 2D-3D bounding boxes, object categories, hand information (i.e., hand side, contact state, and associated active objects) and also multimodal signals such as depth maps and instance segmentation masks.

Using the proposed pipeline, we present EgoISM-HOI (Egocentric Industrial Synthetic Multimodal dataset for Human-Object Interaction detection). This is a new photo-realistic dataset of EHOIs in an industrial scenario, and it has rich annotations of hands, objects, and active objects (i.e., the objects the user is interacting with), including class labels, depth maps, and instance segmentation masks (see Fig. 1 (b)). We also want to check if the synthetic data generated with the proposed protocol is suitable for the EHOI detection task on target real data. For this we acquired and labeled 42 real egocentric videos in an industrial laboratory, where different subjects perform test and repair operations on electrical boards. We annotated all the EHOI instances of the images, identifying the frames where interactions happen and all the active objects with a bounding box with the related object class. We also labeled the hands and all the objects in the images.

We investigated if the generated synthetic multimodal data, including depth maps and instance segmentation masks, can be used to improve the performance of EHOI detection methods. In particular, we designed an EHOI detection approach based on an existing method, which uses the different multimodal signals that are available in our dataset. The experiments show that the proposed method outperforms baseline approaches that exploit class-agnostic models trained on out-of-domain real-world data. The proposed method achieves good performance when it is trained with our synthetic data and a very small amount of real-world data. Additional experiments show that the accuracy and robustness of our EHOI detection system increased when multimodal signals are used.

The contributions of this study are: 1) a pipeline that uses 3D models of real objects and environments to generate thousands of domain-specific synthetic egocentric human-object interaction images, together with several labels and modalities; 2) EgoISM-HOI, a new multimodal dataset of synthetic EHOIs in an industrial scenario with rich annotations of hands and objects. We also acquire and manually label real-world images of EHOIs in the target environment, to test if models can generalize to real-world data; 3) a new method for EHOI detection that uses additional modalities, such as depth maps and instance segmentation maps, to improve the performance of classic HOI detection approaches; 4) extensive evaluations that show the benefit of using synthetic data to pre-train EHOI detection methods, mostly when only a limited set of real data is available, and the improvements of our approach over classical class-agnostic state-of-the-art methods; 5) we release the dataset and the code publicly at this link: https://iplab.dmi.unict.it/egoism-hoi.

The rest of the paper is organized like this. Section 2 summarizes the related work. Section 3 describes the proposed data generation pipeline. Section 4 describes the proposed dataset. Section 5 introduces our multimodal EHOI detection method. Section 6 reports and discusses the experiments and ablation studies. Section 7 concludes the paper.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
In recent years, wearable devices have become increasingly popular since they offer a first-person perspective of how users interact with the world around them. One advantage of wearable devices is that they allow visual information to be collected and processed without requiring users to hold any device in their hands, so that they can perform their activities in a natural way. Intelligent systems can analyze this visual information to provide services supporting humans in different domains such as activities of daily living [1,2,3], cultural sites [4] and industrial scenarios [5,6]. In particular, egocentric vision can be adopted in the industrial context to understand workers' behavior, improve workplace safety, and increase overall productivity. For example, by detecting the hands of the workers and determining which objects they are interacting with, it is possible to monitor object usage, provide information on the procedures to be carried out, and improve worker safety by issuing reminders when dangerous objects are manipulated.

Previous works have investigated the problem of Human-Object Interaction detection (HOI) from either third-person [7,8] or first-person [9,10] points of view. While these works have considered generic scenarios (e.g., COCO objects) or class-agnostic settings [11], their use in industrial contexts is still understudied due to the limited availability of public datasets [12,5]. Developing a system capable of detecting Egocentric Human-Object Interactions (EHOI) in this context generally requires collecting and labeling large amounts of domain-specific data, which can be expensive in terms of costs and time and is not always possible due to privacy constraints and industrial secrets [12].

In this paper, we investigate whether the use of synthetic data in first-person vision can mitigate the need for labeled real domain-specific data in model training, which would greatly reduce the cost of gathering a suitable dataset for model development. We propose a pipeline (see Fig. 1) and a tool that leverage 3D models of the target environment and objects to produce a large number of synthetic EHOI image examples. These are automatically labeled with several annotations, such as hand-object 2D-3D bounding boxes, object categories, hand information (i.e., hand side, contact state, and associated active objects) as well as multimodal signals such as depth maps and instance segmentation masks.

Exploiting the proposed pipeline, we present EgoISM-HOI (Egocentric Industrial Synthetic Multimodal dataset for Human-Object Interaction detection), a new photo-realistic dataset of EHOIs in an industrial scenario with rich annotations of hands, objects, and active objects (i.e., the objects the user is interacting with), including class labels, depth maps, and instance segmentation masks (see Fig. 1 (b)). To assess whether the synthetic data generated with the proposed protocol is suitable for tackling the EHOI detection task on target real data, we also acquired and labeled 42 real egocentric videos in an industrial laboratory in which different subjects perform test and repair operations on electrical boards. We annotated all EHOI instances in the images, identifying the frames in which interactions occur and all active objects with a bounding box associated with the related object class. In addition, we labeled the hands and all the objects in the images.

We investigated the potential of the generated synthetic multimodal data, including depth maps and instance segmentation masks, to improve the performance of EHOI detection methods. Specifically, we designed an EHOI detection approach based on the method proposed in [11] which makes use of the different multimodal signals available in our dataset. Experiments show that the proposed method outperforms baseline approaches that exploit class-agnostic models trained on out-of-domain real-world data. Indeed, the proposed method achieves good performance when trained with our synthetic data and a very small amount of real-world data. Additional experiments show that leveraging multimodal signals increased the accuracy and robustness of our EHOI detection system.

The contributions of this study are the following: 1) we propose a pipeline that exploits 3D models of real objects and environments to generate thousands of domain-specific synthetic egocentric human-object interaction images paired with several labels and modalities; 2) we present EgoISM-HOI, a new multimodal dataset of synthetic EHOIs in an industrial scenario with rich annotations of hands and objects. To test the ability of models to generalize to real-world data, we acquire and manually label real-world images of EHOIs in the target environment; 3) we design a new method for EHOI detection that exploits additional modalities, such as depth maps and instance segmentation maps, to enhance the performance of classic HOI detection approaches; 4) we perform extensive evaluations highlighting the benefit of using synthetic data to pre-train EHOI detection methods, mainly when a limited set of real data is available, and report improvements of our approach over classical class-agnostic state-of-the-art methods; 5) we publicly release the dataset and code at the following link: https://iplab.dmi.unict.it/egoism-hoi.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 summarizes the related work. Section 3 details the proposed data generation pipeline. Section 4 describes the proposed dataset. Section 5 introduces our multimodal EHOI detection method. Section 6 reports and discusses the experiments and ablation studies. Finally, Section 7 concludes the paper.
